text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's Austrian newspapers:
- Following a reform of Austrian trade regulations, local inns will be allowed to sell groceries if there is not another grocer in the town.

- A new telecommunications law should be ready by mid-May. According to the draft, competitors to current monopoly Post and Telekom will have to pay a fee for offering universal services once the sector is liberalised.
- Austria has the third-highest per capita savings rate in Europe, a new study shows.

- Andreas Khol, chief whip of the conservative junior coalition partner People's Party, says Social Democrat Chancellor Viktor Klima supports conservative Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel's views on Austria's future security policy. Work on a report on Austria's options should start immediately, he says.
- The conservatives reject setting up a parliamentary enquiry to investigate the suicide last weekend of Gerhard Praschak, board member of clearing bank OeKB.

- The People's Party wants to see first results of a reform of Austria's pension system reflected in the 1998/99 budget, but the Social Affairs Ministry says its own ideas for a reform will not have any effect before the start of the new millenium.
- European Union plans to introduce a unified energy tax could double energy taxes in Austria, industrialists say.
- A German consortium led by construction groups Stuag and Rhomberg says it has good chances of winning the tender to build the Semmering rail tunnel in eastern Austria.

- Interior Minister Karl Schloegl will on Tuesday present a new draft immegration law. The overall number of immigrants will remain limited, but the extradition of foreigners already living in Austria should become more difficult.
- Wolfgang Ruttenstorfer, state secretary of finance, says he wants to abolish all corporate tax loopholes.
